turns.text: Sir, field report number two on the electricity file. Today: where electricity is made.. and how it gets home. Last time we learned it's charge moving in a wire. Today: who moves it? And from where? Strangest thing I found: the power lighting their lamps right now.. was made less than a second ago. No warehouse. What's made is used that instant. Billions of humans, each pressing switches whenever they like.. and someone must supply exactly that, at that instant. No more, no less.

turns.text: In eighteen thirty-one, an Englishman named Faraday found something simple: move a magnet past a wire.. and its electrons move. Spin the magnet inside a coil of wire, and it keeps pushing the electrons. Back.. and forth. That's a generator. So naturally, it makes AC. A motor is the same machine in reverse: feed it power.. it spins. The fan, the washing machine, the electric car: generators running backwards. Faraday was a blacksmith's son who left school early. A bookbinder's apprentice.. who read what he bound. Their greatest invention: a guy reading on the job. One question left: who turns the magnet? They mount it on a giant fan called a turbine. Since Faraday, most of the planet's power is made this same way. All that changes: what turns the turbine.

turns.text: Their favorite way: boil water. Burn coal or gas under a boiler the size of a building. Steam spins the turbine. The turbine spins the generator. Out comes electricity. The nuclear plant, sir? The most complex thing they ever built. They split the atom itself. To boil water. A fingertip of nuclear fuel holds about a ton of coal's energy. Countries with volcanoes take steam straight from underground. Still steam. This planet is addicted to kettles. So kind one is steam: coal, gas, nuclear. Kind two is water: a high dam, the water falls onto the turbine. The planet's biggest station.. a dam in China. Kind three is wind: turbines the wind keeps turning. The one exception: the solar panel. Nothing spins at all. Light knocks the electrons and moves them. And it makes direct current. Here's each one's share of the planet's power in twenty twenty-five. Coal still first: a third. Then gas. Then dams, nuclear, solar and wind. But that year, for the first time in a century: all renewables together.. passed coal. By a hair. Solar alone was about one percent ten years ago. Now nearly nine. Their fastest-growing source.. is the only one that doesn't spin.

turns.text: Now let's follow the power. The generator makes it at about twenty thousand volts. First stop: a transformer lifts it to hundreds of thousands. A transformer has no moving parts. Two coils of wire around iron. More turns on one side.. so the pressure comes out higher there. That's it. Then it travels on tall towers. Hundreds of kilometers. Near the city, another transformer brings it down. Then smaller ones on the streets. Until it enters the house at one-ten or two-forty volts. Depends on the country. Humans agreed on volts, amps and ohms. But the plug itself? About fifteen kinds. Every traveler carries a little piece of plastic.. whose job is peace between two countries. The trip takes less than a blink. The only thing here that's on time. Why raise the pressure, then lower it? Because current heats the wire. The bigger the current, the more power lost as heat. The same power can be sent two ways: low pressure, big current.. or high pressure, small current. The second loses far less. Like moving a thousand passengers. A thousand small cars jam the road and burn fuel. Or one fast train. High voltage is the train. And the transformer only works on alternating current. That's the real reason Tesla beat Edison. Even so, some is lost on the way. In America, about five percent. In countries with old or weak grids, much more. And some of what's lost there isn't lost.. it's stolen. A warning for command: high-voltage lines are bare, no jacket. The air insulates them. Get close, even without touching, and the power can jump to you. Humans hang a skull on them. They're right.

turns.text: A question their children ask: the bird on that bare wire.. why doesn't it get shocked? Both its feet are on the same wire. Current flows when there's a pressure difference between two points. Both feet are at the same pressure. So no current goes through it. But if it touches another wire, or anything grounded, at the same moment.. it becomes the path. And humans stand on the ground all the time. So that rule is for birds only. That's also why towers are so tall, and wires hang far apart and far from everything. The distance itself insulates.

He lets a joke land flat and never laughs at it. The central idea of the report: a balance kept every second. Clear, a little awed, then a funny true story.
turns.text: Back to the big problem. The grid can't store power. So what stations make must equal what people draw. Every second. One number tells them if the balance is right: the frequency. Generator turns per second. Fifty on most of the planet, sixty in North America. People draw more than is made? The generators get heavier, slow down. The number drops. Control orders a station up. The number comes back. All day long, nobody notices. Every grid has a control room, people at screens twenty-four hours a day. Their whole job: keep that number at fifty. The planet's most important workers.. and nobody knows their names. The generators help too. Each is hundreds of tonnes of spinning iron. If something fails, the weight keeps spinning a few seconds.. buying the grid time. If a big station drops out and the number falls fast? The grid cuts whole districts by itself. It sacrifices a part.. so the whole doesn't fall. Their whole civilization rests on one number. It must stay fifty. Not forty-nine. It makes for strange moments. In nineteen ninety, England played Germany in the World Cup semi-final. It went to penalties. The match ended.. and the whole country got up at once to switch on the kettle. Demand jumped two thousand eight hundred megawatts in minutes. Two big power stations. Still their record. Their grid engineers have studied the TV schedule ever since. They know when the show ends, and have a station ready for that second. England lost the match. The grid won.

turns.text: Grids grew and joined up. Europe: one grid from Portugal to Turkey. Over four hundred million people. Every generator in it turns together. Same speed, same instant. Thousands of machines.. like one machine. That makes it stronger: a station fails in one country, the neighbours cover. It also makes the neighbours' problems.. yours. They trade power every hour. A windy country sells today.. and buys tomorrow. In twenty eighteen, Kosovo and Serbia argued over who should make up missing power. The whole grid slowed a hair. Instead of fifty: forty-nine point nine nine six. Oven clocks and alarm clocks, which count time from the grid's pulse, fell six minutes behind. In twenty-five countries. A quarrel between two.. made a whole continent late for work. Finally, a scientific excuse. Japan is the opposite. In eighteen ninety-five, Tokyo bought German generators turning at fifty. The next year, Osaka bought American ones at sixty. To this day the country is split in two, joined only by special converter stations. In twenty eleven, after the great earthquake, the east needed power and the west had extra. Only a trickle could cross the link. Tokyo had rolling blackouts. A purchase made over a century ago.

turns.text: Demand changes through the day. Low at dawn, rising in the morning, highest after sunset.. when everyone gets home and switches everything on. So some stations run all the time, and others sit idle and run just two hours a day. For the peak. Their power is the most expensive. The year's top peak comes with a heat wave, every air conditioner at once. Or a cold snap. So the grid is built for the worst hour of the year.. and half of it sits idle the rest of the time. That's why in many countries power prices change by the hour. A washing machine at midnight.. costs less than one at sunset.

turns.text: Two words from the human dictionary. Hertz: turns per second. The grid's pulse. And megawatt: a million watts. Enough for hundreds of homes. Or one small data center.

turns.text: Report summary, sir. One: a generator is a spinning magnet, and nearly every station is looking for something to spin it. Two: the voltage goes up so power can travel, and comes down before the house. Three: what's made must equal what's drawn. Every second. Same warning: any wire in the street, fallen or hanging, nobody goes near it. Keep away.. and report it. Next report: what happens when this balance breaks? Why the lights go out, and how one tree darkened fifty million people. This was Earth Report. Agent Peek. Transmission ends.
